repos.title: KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU
repos.paper_summary:
KVMem is a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed agent workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. Instead of compacting older context into lossy text summaries or retrieving it as text for repeated prefill, KVMem materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model’s native context window. It uses step-level memory scheduling to update the historical working set once per agent step, query-conditioned retrieval via compact Mean-K indexes derived from the serving model’s attention space, and tiered KV management with position-consistent re-RoPE to restore selected blocks efficiently.

On LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, KVMem generally achieves higher task utility than compaction-based approaches and reduces post-compaction recovery latency by 11.4–53.8× compared to Compact+RAG. In a DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% to 48.4%. On a consumer laptop with a 24 GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, KVMem supports a 1M-token virtual workspace—four times the model’s 256K-token context window—while sustaining approximately 50 tokens/s in single-session generation. Limitations include the fact that reused KV state is not mathematically equivalent to recomputing text under new contexts, and that retrieval may miss task-relevant blocks if the active execution view is too small.

repos.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
repos.paper_summary:
Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. It provides a persistent IPython REPL, recursive subagents with direct agent-to-agent communication, and Continual Harness for storing versioned prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications across trajectories. The model controls strategy construction while the runtime standardizes execution, recovery, and resource accounting.

The paper evaluates Prime Agent against native and alternative harnesses (Pi, Claude Code, Codex) on interactive reasoning, long-context tasks, and autonomous systems construction. On ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent raises RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%. In long-context benchmarks, it matches or exceeds baselines; for example, on OOLONG (Yahoo, 128k), GPT-5.6 Sol scores .940 with Prime Agent versus .900 with Codex. For GPU kernel generation on PMPP-Hard, Prime Agent achieves comparable solve rates at substantially reduced token cost. A seven-day Factorio run completed 24 of 196 technologies using 23.4 million output tokens. Limitations include models' poor handling of irreversible actions and online refinement potentially preserving specification exploits as reusable skills.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent argues the harness should expose expressive primitives, so evaluation measures model capability rather than harness failures.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Prime Agent Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent splits information management from computation management across persistent sessions, a daemon and Continual Harness state.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent is generally competitive on long-context tasks and close to native harnesses on GPU-kernel generation.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work spans programmatic inference, coding-agent runtimes, ARC-AGI-3 systems and multi-agent communication, which Prime Agent combines.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Many harness capabilities remain underused because current models were not trained to operate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists three out-of-loop nanoGPT experiments, from Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and a third model, plus an orchestration example.

repos.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
repos.paper_summary:
ChatDev is a multi-agent software development framework that uses LLM-driven agents to execute design, coding, and testing phases through structured dialogue. The system organizes work via a "chat chain," which breaks tasks into subtasks handled by pairs of agents acting as instructor and assistant. A "communicative dehallucination" mechanism reduces errors by having the assistant request specific details before generating code.

Evaluated on a dataset of 1,200 software requirements, ChatDev outperforms GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT. In Table 1, ChatDev achieves an executability score of 0.880 and a quality score of 0.395, compared to 0.415 and 0.152 for MetaGPT. Pairwise evaluations in Table 2 show ChatDev winning 77.1% of comparisons against GPT-Engineer when judged by GPT-4. Ablations in Table 4 indicate that removing agent roles drops executability from 0.880 to 0.580. Limitations include high computational costs due to multiple agents and a tendency to generate simple logic or static placeholders rather than complex database interactions, making it suitable primarily for prototypes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev uses chat among role-playing LLM agents, with language as the shared medium, across design, coding, and testing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers LLM agents and deep learning applied to single waterfall phases, which the authors say remain isolated.

digest_headlines.heading: ChatDev
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev pairs an instructor agent and an assistant agent per subtask, linked by a chat chain and dehallucination rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev scores highest on all four metrics and wins most pairwise comparisons against GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Authors conclude that language-based multi-agent communication improves software optimization and supports agent autonomy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Agents need detailed requirements, evaluation covers limited dimensions, and multi-agent runs need more tokens and time.

repos.title: LeRobot: An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
repos.paper_summary:
`lerobot` is an open-source Python library for end-to-end robot learning that integrates low-level motor control, data collection, and policy training. It supports eight hardware platforms, including the SO-100 and ALOHA-2, using a shared middleware API for teleoperation. The library introduces `LeRobotDataset`, a standardized format for multimodal robotics data that enables streaming large datasets without full downloads. As of September 2025, the ecosystem includes over 16,000 datasets from 2,200 contributors.

The library provides PyTorch implementations of leading algorithms such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0}$, and SmolVLA. Inference benchmarks on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 show ACT achieving 5.01 ms latency, while the larger $\pi_{0}$ model requires 209 ms. An asynchronous inference stack decouples action prediction from execution, allowing policies to run on remote machines. Limitations include incomplete coverage of robot embodiments and algorithms, and the lack of low-level optimizations like quantization or graph compilation for practical deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Robot learning tools are fragmented, so the authors present lerobot, an open-source library spanning the full stack from motor control to datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Low-cost open arms cost a fraction of industrial ones, and this accessibility supports decentralized data collection.

digest_headlines.heading: Features
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot supports several low-cost arms, a shared dataset format with 16K+ datasets, and reference implementations of policies.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation is used only for benchmarking, since the authors find simulation challenging for the contact-rich tasks the library targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot is presented as a unified open stack, with limits in robot coverage, algorithm count, and inference optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists robot build guides, dataset breakdowns, the streaming dataset design, model and inference examples, and a synchronous versus asynchronous comparison.

repos.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
repos.paper_summary:
DSPy is a programming model that compiles declarative language model pipelines into self-improving systems by automatically optimizing prompts and demonstrations. It replaces hard-coded prompt strings with parameterized modules, such as `ChainOfThought` or `ReAct`, which are optimized by "teleprompters." These optimizers bootstrap few-shot examples or finetune smaller models to maximize a user-defined metric.

On the GSM8K math word problem dataset, compiled DSPy programs using GPT-3.5 achieved 81.6% test accuracy, outperforming standard few-shot prompting (72.4%) and expert-created demonstrations (72.4%). For llama2-13b-chat, the best configuration reached 46.9% test accuracy, surpassing the zero-shot baseline of 9.4%. On HotPotQA multi-hop question answering, a compiled multi-hop program with GPT-3.5 achieved 45.6% answer exact match, while a finetuned T5-Large model reached 39.3% on the development set. The paper notes that compiling typically takes minutes to tens of minutes. Limitations include reliance on specific metrics for optimization and the fact that results are reported on only two case studies.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hand-written prompt templates for LM pipelines are brittle, and the paper proposes DSPy to replace them with optimizable modules.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing toolkits rely on hand-written prompt templates, while DSPy aims to optimize arbitrary multi-stage LM pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Programming Model
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy programs combine typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that optimize all modules against a metric.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Compiler
digest_headlines.headline: The compiler runs three stages: bootstrapping candidate demonstrations, selecting among them, and optimizing control flow.

digest_headlines.heading: Goals of Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation hypothesizes that DSPy can replace hand-written prompts without losing quality, adapt across LMs, and enable richer pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Math Word Problems
digest_headlines.headline: Compiled DSPy programs improve GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat on math word problems from 4–20% accuracy to 49–88%.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Complex Question Answering
digest_headlines.headline: On HotPotQA, a multihop program compiled with ensembling reaches 54.7 dev answer exact match with GPT-3.5.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy supports rapid development of effective systems with small LMs, and wider task reporting is deferred to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers advanced signatures, a comparison with LangChain and LlamaIndex, and long prompts from existing libraries and DSPy.

repos.title: ReasoningShield: Safety Detection over Reasoning Traces of Large Reasoning Models
repos.paper_summary: ReasoningShield is a benchmark and a pair of lightweight moderation models for detecting safety risks in the reasoning traces (chain-of-thought, CoT) of large reasoning models, rather than only in final answers. The benchmark has 9.2K annotated (Query, CoT) pairs: a 7K-sample training split and a 2.2K human-annotated test split, covering 10 risk categories, 3 safety levels, and 8 LRMs. On a pilot set, existing tools such as LlamaGuard-4 lost up to 35.2 F1 points when moderating CoTs instead of answers. The authors train 1B and 3B models with supervised fine-tuning on consensus-labeled samples (about 4K), then direct preference optimization on about 3K hard negatives. ReasoningShield-3B reaches 91.8% F1 on the benchmark, versus 35.6 points above LlamaGuard-4 and 15.8 points above GPT-4o. The paper also reports generalization to out-of-distribution sources, cross-task settings, and adversarial attacks. Labels were produced by a three-model ensemble with majority voting, with a human-annotated test set reaching Fleiss' κ = 0.75. Limitations: the work covers content safety only, not agentic risks such as tool misuse, and it is limited to English-language and text-only settings as described.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Reasoning traces can hide harm that final answers conceal, and existing moderators drop sharply on them.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior safety work and moderators target question-answer data, leaving reasoning traces without structured benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Safety detection over reasoning traces
digest_headlines.headline: Existing moderators lose F1 on reasoning traces, with LlamaGuard-4 reaching only 29.3% on Grok-3 traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Construction of ReasoningShield
digest_headlines.headline: The authors build a ten-category, three-level risk taxonomy and label 7,000 training traces with a model ensemble and human-checked test traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and results
digest_headlines.headline: ReasoningShield-3B reaches 91.8% F1 on open-source reasoning traces, above GPT-4o's 87.8% under the authors' prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and future works
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that the benchmark exposes a moderation gap and state that agentic safety is out of scope.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers ethics and access terms, risk definitions, annotation and efficiency details, and per-category and stability analyses.

repos.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
repos.paper_summary:
AutoGen is an open-source framework for building LLM applications via multi-agent conversations. The system defines two core concepts: conversable agents, which are customizable entities backed by LLMs, tools, or human inputs, and conversation programming, a method that structures application logic around inter-agent message passing and control flow. Agents use unified interfaces to send messages and generate replies, with an auto-reply mechanism driving the workflow without a central controller. Developers can program interaction patterns using Python code or natural language instructions embedded in agent prompts.

The paper evaluates AutoGen across six domains. On the MATH dataset (5000 problems), the default two-agent configuration achieved 69.48% accuracy, outperforming vanilla GPT-4 at 55.18%. In ALFWorld decision-making tasks, adding a "grounding" agent improved performance by 15% over a ReAct baseline. For coding tasks on OptiGuide, a multi-agent design increased the F-1 score for identifying unsafe code by 8% with GPT-4 and 35% with GPT-3.5-turbo compared to a single-agent setup. The framework reduced the core workflow code for one application from 430 lines to 100 lines. Limitations include the reliance on proprietary models like GPT-4 for peak performance and the lack of formal safety guarantees for fully autonomous agent interactions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent conversation is proposed as the basis for building LLM applications, implemented in the AutoGen framework.

digest_headlines.heading: The AutoGen Framework
digest_headlines.headline: AutoGen rests on conversable agents and conversation programming, where agents exchange messages and control flow emerges from those conversations.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications of AutoGen
digest_headlines.headline: Six example applications test AutoGen across math, retrieval, decision making, coding, group chat and chess.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The discussion frames AutoGen as a general framework and states that its experiments are early, with safety questions left open.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: The ethics statement names privacy, bias, accountability, trust and unintended consequences as risks to address.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work with a comparison table, expanded discussion, usage guidelines, future work, and supporting figures.

repos.title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
repos.paper_summary: cuRoboV2-Fast is a GPU-accelerated motion planner for collision-free, torque-limited robot motions that reduces planning latency and execution time. It combines a bounded bidirectional RRT for route initialization, B-spline trajectory optimization with parallel evaluation and gradient gathering, TimeOpt (a solver that retimes a fixed path under velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque bounds), and differentiable inverse dynamics that accept payload changes without recompiling. On 2,575 MotionBenchMaker and MPINets queries, its RRT reaches 98.68% initialization success at 0.305 ms mean planning time, versus 91.92% for cuRoboV1 PRM and 88.27% for cuRoboV2 PRM. With a 3 kg payload on an RTX 5090, mean planning time is 4.43 ms, 14.7× faster than cuRoboV2. TimeOpt cuts mean motion time by 15.7% relative to the refined trajectory. Success stays near cuRoboV2 across payloads and exceeds the TOPPRA baselines by 14.5–15.7 percentage points at the heaviest payload. TimeOpt finds a local minimum and does not guarantee global optimality. Its advantage is shown on Franka Panda and YAM setups.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Planning time and execution time both matter, and cuRoboV2-Fast targets both for payload-aware, torque-limited motions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers parallel planners, B-spline refinement, and fixed-path timing, and the method builds on each.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: The planner fits B-spline trajectories to a parallel tree-search seed, then retimes them with TimeOpt under payload-dependent torque limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show lower planning and motion times than cuRoboV2 at similar success, with real-robot gains in arm execution time.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Fewer iterations, cheaper iterations, and TimeOpt timing drive the gains, while planning is only 1.0% of real-robot cycle time.

repos.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
repos.paper_summary: The Switch Transformer replaces the standard feed-forward layer in Transformers with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module that routes each token to a single expert, reducing communication overhead and improving training stability. By using top-1 routing instead of top-k, the model maintains constant computational cost per token while scaling parameter count. The paper introduces selective precision casting to stabilize bfloat16 training and an auxiliary load-balancing loss to ensure uniform expert usage. Experiments on the C4 corpus show that a 64-expert Switch-Base model achieves the same pre-training quality as T5-Base in one-seventh the time. Fine-tuning results indicate consistent improvements over T5-Base and T5-Large on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and summarization tasks. Distilling these sparse models into dense T5-Base architectures preserves approximately 30% of the quality gain while compressing model size by up to 99%. In multilingual settings across 101 languages, the method yields a mean 5x speedup over mT5-Base. A limitation is that distillation does not fully recover teacher performance, and the approach relies on specific hardware parallelism strategies for trillion-parameter scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse expert routing is proposed to add parameters without raising per-example compute, with gains across pre-training, fine-tuning and multilingual training.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch Transformer
digest_headlines.headline: Routing each token to one expert simplifies Mixture of Experts, with capacity limits and a balancing loss keeping training stable.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Properties
digest_headlines.headline: Increasing experts at fixed FLOPS per token speeds up pre-training, with Switch-Base 64 reaching T5-Base quality in one-seventh the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Downstream Results
digest_headlines.headline: Switch models improve most T5 fine-tuning tasks, distill to dense models keeping 30% of gains, and beat mT5 on all 101 languages.

digest_headlines.heading: Designing Models with Data, Model, and Expert-Parallelism
digest_headlines.headline: Data, model and expert parallelism combine to train 395 billion and 1.6 trillion parameter Switch models, with Switch-XXL sometimes unstable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work scales models through model parallelism and conditional computation, including mixture of experts and attention sparsity.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse models are argued to outperform dense models per step and on wall clock time, but distilled versions keep only about 30% of gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining challenges include stabilizing the largest models, heterogeneous experts, expert layers beyond feed-forward layers, and other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switch Transformers are presented as stable, sample-efficient language learners across pre-training, fine-tuning and multi-task training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers attention Switch layers, token rerouting, router exploration, small-scale results, upstream-downstream correlation and pseudocode.

repos.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
repos.paper_summary: Co-Design Bench is a reference-free benchmark for coding agents that revise real users' web applications from multimodal requests. It contains 273 tasks drawn from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real coding sessions, split into Multimodal Editing (100 tasks, optional image, audio, video, or document inputs) and Repository Editing (173 tasks, coordinated multi-file changes). Each task has a runnable pre-edit app and hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria (2,331 in total). Grading is a "judge-then-refute" protocol: a fixed LLM evaluator assigns Pass, Partial, or Fail per criterion from source diffs, renders, and browser traces, then a separate LLM verifier challenges positive verdicts. Under a shared Claude Code harness, the strongest of ten endpoints (gpt-6-astra) reaches a mean strict criterion completion of 0.699 but fully completes only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints score lower on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. A limitation is that tasks evaluate a fixed request without simulated user feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench tests whether coding agents turn real users' multimodal revision requests into working application changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks cover screenshot reconstruction, predefined edits, and repository issues, but few cover compound revisions drawn from real coding sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Co-Design Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each task pairs a runnable pre-edit application with a normalized request, attachments, and hidden expert-authored criteria.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Protocol
digest_headlines.headline: A judge grades each criterion from source and browser evidence, then a separate verifier challenges positive verdicts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across ten endpoints, criterion coverage runs well ahead of complete delivery, with the top model fully passing 26.4% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench offers a shared setting for measuring complete delivery, with runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence retained.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the WebCompass execution-regime comparison, evaluator sensitivity, resource accounting, cases, dataset composition, and evaluation details.
